reports.surface: MJPG-streamer setup: scripts/mjpg-launcher.sh, scripts/tune-mjpg.sh, scripts/mjpg-streamer.service, scripts/mjpg-streamer-auto.service, scripts/start-mjpg-auto.sh, scripts/install-mjpg-streamer-integration.sh, scripts/setup-mjpg-streamer-service.sh, scripts/setup-webcam.sh, scripts/install-webcam-watchdog.sh + scripts/webcam-watchdog.{sh,service}, scripts/mjpg-streamer-watchdog.sh + scripts/install-mjpg-streamer-watchdog.sh, install.sh (Step 14 + line 412), controllers/webcamController.js (drop-in writer + proxy client), config read: /etc/default/monsterbox-cam (node-local, not in repo)

findings.title: (a) Flag matrix: eight competing launch configs; canonical is 640x480@15 q60, but install.sh's own tune step overrides it to 24fps q80 hardcoded /dev/video0
findings.evidence: Canonical launcher: /home/user/MonsterBox/scripts/mjpg-launcher.sh:27-29 (input_uvc -r 640x480 -f 15 -q 60, stable /dev/v4l/by-id device, overridable via /etc/default/monsterbox-cam read at :16). install.sh installs a unit running that launcher (/home/user/MonsterBox/install.sh:322-337) — but then install.sh:411-412 runs tune-mjpg.sh with '/dev/video0 640x480 24 80', and /home/user/MonsterBox/scripts/tune-mjpg.sh:19-26 writes systemd drop-in /etc/systemd/system/mjpg-streamer.service.d/20-monsterbox-vid.conf that RESETS ExecStart to a hardcoded '/dev/video0 ... -f 24 -q 80' line. So every fresh install ends at 24fps q80 on a bare device node, silently discarding both the 15fps operator spec and the by-id self-healing (the exact crash-loop the launcher exists to prevent, per its own comment mjpg-launcher.sh:4-9). Other writers of the SAME unit file with different flags: scripts/mjpg-streamer.service:15 (15fps q75 + -n -n), scripts/install-mjpg-streamer-integration.sh:79 (15fps q85), scripts/setup-mjpg-streamer-service.sh:65 (15fps q85), scripts/setup-webcam.sh unit (15fps q85, Type=forking), scripts/start-mjpg-auto.sh:39-41 (30fps q70 + -n -n) via scripts/mjpg-streamer-auto.service:11, and controllers/webcamController.js:733-745 (part-config or default q85) writing a SECOND drop-in override.conf. Last writer wins; drop-ins beat unit files; override.conf beats 20-monsterbox-vid.conf (lexical order). What actually runs on sirdragomir is unknowable from the repo — readActiveStreamGeometry (webcamController.js:451-499) exists precisely because of this.
findings.estimatedCost: 24fps vs 15fps = +60% producer frame rate and +60% USB/loopback/WiFi bandwidth per client for zero operator benefit (spec at mjpg-launcher.sh:11-13 is phone monitoring). At MJPEG passthrough CPU stays ~0.1-1% of one core (measured 0.1% on Orlok: docs/evidence/v11-audit-2026-08-21/v11-uptime-perf.md:5), so the fps bump costs little CPU on the streamer itself — its damage is downstream: a faster producer makes every non-dropping consumer (TCP socket, Node proxy) fall behind 60% faster and deepens any standing frame queue proportionally. The hardcoded /dev/video0 in the drop-in re-arms the documented 42-restart crash-loop on the next USB re-enumeration.
findings.fix: Delete install.sh:411-413 (the tune-mjpg call) and delete/neuter scripts/tune-mjpg.sh; make anything that wants per-node geometry write /etc/default/monsterbox-cam (MB_CAM_DEV/RES/FPS/Q) which the launcher already sources, then `systemctl restart mjpg-streamer`. On sirdragomir: `systemctl cat mjpg-streamer` and `rm -rf /etc/systemd/system/mjpg-streamer.service.d`, daemon-reload, restart, confirm ps shows '-f 15 -q 60' and a by-id -d path.

findings.title: (a) Input format: MJPEG-native is requested (no -y anywhere), but the jacksonliam experimental build all installers compile SILENTLY falls back to YUYV + per-frame software JPEG encode if the camera/mode lacks MJPEG
findings.evidence: No launch line passes -y: mjpg-launcher.sh:28, tune-mjpg.sh:26, mjpg-streamer.service:15, start-mjpg-auto.sh:40, install-mjpg-streamer-integration.sh:79, setup-mjpg-streamer-service.sh:65, webcamController.js:745 — input_uvc.so defaults to V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG. All installers build github.com/jacksonliam/mjpg-streamer experimental from source (install.sh:306-311, install-mjpg-streamer-integration.sh:49-52, setup-webcam.sh clone block), and that fork's input_uvc falls back to YUYV with software compression (using the -q value) when the camera can't deliver MJPEG at the requested mode — it logs the fallback to the journal but keeps running, so nothing in these scripts would notice. Note: with true MJPEG passthrough, -q is IGNORED, so the q60/75/80/85 wars across the eight configs change nothing unless the node is secretly in YUYV fallback.
findings.estimatedCost: MJPEG passthrough: ~0.1-1% of one core (matches Orlok's measured 0.1%). YUYV fallback at 640x480: software JPEG encode on a Cortex-A72 costs roughly 20-40% of one core at 15fps, 35-60% at 24fps — a real dent on a 4-core Pi also running node, OpenCV, and a servo daemon, and it doubles as latency (encode time added per frame). Verification on the node is one command: `top -p $(pidof mjpg_streamer)` (>10% = YUYV) or `journalctl -u mjpg-streamer | grep -i 'YUV\|fallback\|pixelformat'`.
findings.fix: On sirdragomir, check the journal for the YUYV fallback line and `v4l2-ctl -d <dev> --list-formats` for MJPG support at 640x480. If the camera is YUYV-only at that mode, drop to a resolution/fps where it does MJPEG, or accept YUYV but cap fps at 10-15 via /etc/default/monsterbox-cam. Consider adding an explicit startup log/health field 'format: MJPG|YUYV' to probeMjpgStreamer's report so silent fallback becomes visible.

findings.title: (b) Two differently-named systemd units both claim port 8090 and can stack: mjpg-streamer.service + mjpg-streamer-auto.service, both Restart=always
findings.evidence: scripts/mjpg-streamer-auto.service:11 runs scripts/start-mjpg-auto.sh (30fps q70, auto-detect device) on port 8090 (start-mjpg-auto.sh:41); scripts/mjpg-streamer.service:15 also binds 8090. Both declare Restart=always (mjpg-streamer-auto.service:12, mjpg-streamer.service:16). Nothing in the repo installs or disables the -auto unit (grep for 'mjpg-streamer-auto' finds only its own ExecStart line), so it is an orphan that a past hand-install could have left enabled. If both are enabled: the port-bind loser exits and crash-loops every RestartSec=5 forever, and each retry opens/probes the V4L2 device — which can yank the camera from the winner or from the OpenCV tracker mid-stream. Worse, start-mjpg-auto.sh:11-27 auto-detects 'the first USB capture device', so with two cameras (or camera + HDMI grabber) BOTH units run streaming DIFFERENT devices, doubling capture and holding the device motion tracking wants.
findings.estimatedCost: Crash-looping loser: fork/exec + V4L2 open every ~5s ≈ 1-2% CPU average plus journald spam (SD-card writes, real cost per CLAUDE.md storage constraint). Two live instances: double USB bandwidth + double streamer RSS (~2x 8MB) — modest, but the device-theft side effect is what kills the tracker. Diagnosis is one command on the node: `systemctl list-units 'mjpg*'` and `pgrep -a mjpg_streamer` (expect exactly one).
findings.fix: Delete scripts/mjpg-streamer-auto.service and scripts/start-mjpg-auto.sh from the repo (mjpg-launcher.sh already does device auto-detection better, via by-id); on each node: `systemctl disable --now mjpg-streamer-auto 2>/dev/null; rm -f /etc/systemd/system/mjpg-streamer-auto.service`.

findings.title: (b/c) THREE independent restarters plus systemd Restart can act on the same service: systemd auto-restart, mjpg-streamer-watchdog.timer (30s), and webcam-watchdog.service (30s loop) — no coordination, restart ping-pong possible
findings.evidence: Restarter 1: unit-level Restart=always/on-failure (scripts/mjpg-streamer.service:16, install.sh:332 RestartSec=2). Restarter 2: scripts/install-mjpg-streamer-watchdog.sh:44-56 installs a systemd timer firing scripts/mjpg-streamer-watchdog.sh every 30s (OnUnitActiveSec=30s), which restarts mjpg-streamer.service after 3 failed runs (mjpg-streamer-watchdog.sh:74-83); bringup-animatronic.sh:84-85 installs it on every bring-up. Restarter 3: scripts/webcam-watchdog.sh:71-108 is a FOREVER-LOOP service (webcam-watchdog.service:11 Restart=always) checking every 30s and restarting mjpg-streamer after 3 failures (:96-99); installed by scripts/install-webcam-watchdog.sh:24-41. Both watchdogs poll the SAME snapshot URL (mjpg-streamer-watchdog.sh:8, webcam-watchdog.sh:10) but keep separate failure counters (/run/mjpg-watchdog/failcount vs in-process FAILURE_COUNT), so during a slow start (ExecStartPre sleep 3-5s at mjpg-streamer.service:12 / install-mjpg-streamer-integration.sh:78 + camera init) each watchdog can independently observe failure caused by the OTHER's restart and fire again. Additionally each watchdog run costs the streamer a full JPEG snapshot; webcam-watchdog.sh:38 uses 5s curl timeout on a box that is already slow, biasing toward false failures exactly when the Pi is loaded — restarting the stream because the Pi is busy, making the Pi busier.
findings.estimatedCost: Steady state healthy: ~4 snapshot fetches/min (2 watchdogs x retries) — negligible CPU (<0.5%) but each is a forced frame copy. Pathological state (busy Pi or slow camera init): restart storm where the stream is down 6-10s (sleep 3-5 + camera init + client reconnects) out of every 30-90s window; every restart forces the Node MJPEG proxy and every browser to reconnect through the 3-4s health probes in webcamController.js:340-347, so the visible feed freezes repeatedly — which a viewer reports as 'video is behind' and 'machine is slow'.
findings.fix: Keep exactly ONE watchdog (the timer-based one is stateless-per-run and cheaper; webcam-watchdog.sh's PipeWire check at :45-52 is its only unique value and is warning-only anyway). Delete webcam-watchdog.{sh,service} + install-webcam-watchdog.sh, or make install-webcam-watchdog.sh refuse to install when mjpg-streamer-watchdog.timer is enabled. Also raise FAIL_THRESHOLD or add a 'service started <60s ago — skip' guard so a watchdog never counts failures during another restarter's window.

findings.title: (c) scripts/mjpg-streamer.service sets WatchdogSec=30 on a binary that never calls sd_notify — systemd SIGABRTs and restarts mjpg-streamer every ~30 seconds, forever, if this unit is the installed one
findings.evidence: /home/user/MonsterBox/scripts/mjpg-streamer.service:20-21 ('# Watchdog to detect hangs' / 'WatchdogSec=30') with Type=simple (:7) and Restart=always (:16). mjpg_streamer (jacksonliam build, install.sh:306) does not link libsystemd and never sends WATCHDOG=1, so once WatchdogSec is set systemd kills the service with SIGABRT every 30s and restarts it (ExecStartPre sleep 3 at :12 + RestartSec=5 at :17 on top). This exact unit file is actively installed by scripts/install-webcam-watchdog.sh:18 ('sudo cp "$MJPG_SERVICE_FILE" /etc/systemd/system/mjpg-streamer.service'). If sirdragomir ever ran install-webcam-watchdog.sh, its camera stream has been dying and re-initializing every ~30-38s ever since — presenting as a perpetually freezing/lagging preview and a tracker that can never hold the device or the stream.
findings.estimatedCost: Stream up only ~22-27s of every ~35-38s cycle (sleep 3 + USB/UVC re-init 0.5-2s + client reconnect through 3-4s health probes). CPU cost of the churn itself is small (~1-2%), but every cycle forces: full camera re-init over USB, journal writes (SD wear), Node proxy reconnect, browser stall showing a stale frame (perceived multi-second lag), and an OpenCV tracker reading the stream to hit EOF/timeout. One-command diagnosis on the node: `systemctl show mjpg-streamer -p NRestarts,WatchdogUSec` — NRestarts in the hundreds confirms it.
findings.fix: Delete the WatchdogSec=30 line from scripts/mjpg-streamer.service (the snapshot-probing watchdog timer already covers hang detection properly), or replace the file's role entirely: install-webcam-watchdog.sh should stop shipping its own competing unit and leave the install.sh launcher unit alone.

findings.title: (c) setup-webcam.sh writes a unit with Type=forking but launches mjpg_streamer WITHOUT -b: startup never 'completes', systemd times out at 90s, kills it, Restart=always — perpetual 90s up/kill cycle
findings.evidence: /home/user/MonsterBox/scripts/setup-webcam.sh unit block (printed lines: 'Type=forking', 'ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/mjpg_streamer -i "input_uvc.so -d /dev/video0 -r 640x480 -f 15 -q 85" ...', 'Restart=always', 'RestartSec=5'; heredoc starts at setup-webcam.sh:130). mjpg_streamer stays in the foreground unless passed -b/--background, so with Type=forking systemd waits for the main process to fork-and-exit, which never happens; after default TimeoutStartSec=90 the unit is marked failed and killed, then restarted. Camera streams in ~90s bursts with kills in between. Which installer last ran decides whether the node has this unit, the WatchdogSec one, the q85 one, or the launcher one — five writers of the same path exist (install.sh:322, setup-mjpg-streamer-service.sh:52, install-mjpg-streamer-integration.sh:66, install-webcam-watchdog.sh:18, setup-webcam.sh:130).
findings.estimatedCost: If installed: stream dies every 90s (kill + 5s RestartSec + camera re-init); systemd 'start job' pending state can also wedge dependent units. CPU negligible; operational cost is a video feed that freezes every minute and a half and a device that is repeatedly yanked from any OpenCV consumer.
findings.fix: Change Type=forking to Type=simple in setup-webcam.sh (or add -b to ExecStart, but Type=simple is the smaller change) — or better, delete the unit heredoc from setup-webcam.sh and have it reuse the install.sh launcher unit so the fleet has ONE unit definition.

findings.title: (d) The '-n = no-buffer low-latency mode' comments are false: no flag in any config controls buffering; mjpg-streamer drops frames per-client by design, so multi-second lag is manufactured DOWNSTREAM where nothing drops
findings.evidence: scripts/mjpg-streamer.service:14 ('# -n flag enables no-buffer mode for lower latency') and scripts/start-mjpg-auto.sh:36-38 ('Minimize buffering with -n flag (no-buffer mode)') — but in jacksonliam mjpg-streamer, input_uvc -n means 'skip dynctrl initialization' and output_http -n means 'disable command execution'; neither touches buffering. Actual mjpg-streamer latency budget with these flags: input_uvc's fixed 4-buffer V4L2 ring (≤4/fps s = 266ms at 15fps worst case) + output_http per-client thread that always copies the NEWEST frame (frames drop for slow clients at the handoff). So a healthy streamer contributes ~0.1-0.4s max. The 5-second backlog can only accumulate where MJPEG bytes enter a no-drop pipe: the kernel TCP buffers of the 8090 connection feeding controllers/webcamController.js:602+676 (nodeReadable.pipe(res) honors backpressure, pausing reads so the socket receive buffer — Linux autotunes rmem to multi-MB — silently stores 100-200 frames ≈ 4-8s at 24fps/30-60KB), the same pattern in the orchestration proxy, and any OpenCV --stream-url reader that decodes every frame in order instead of draining (flagged in docs/development/BENCH-HANDOFF-2026-08-23.md:13-19). The tune-mjpg drop-in raising fps 15→24 (install.sh:412) feeds that queue 60% faster; the mjpg-side lever is fps, not any -n flag. No config sets any frame-timeout options; the only timeouts present are watchdog curl timeouts (3-5s).
findings.estimatedCost: mjpg-streamer intrinsic: ~70-400ms — cannot explain 5s. Each proxied viewer costs a full-rate duplicate stream over loopback (~0.7-1.5MB/s at 15fps q60, ~1.5-3MB/s at 24 q80) plus one output_http thread and one Node pipe; 3-4 concurrent viewers + a stream-reading tracker ≈ 5-10MB/s aggregate and 4-5 duplicate frame copies per frame — noticeable on WiFi, minor on CPU. The 5s figure itself matches TCP-buffer math almost exactly (6MB autotuned rmem / ~45KB avg frame / 24fps ≈ 5.5s).
findings.fix: On the mjpg side: pin fps back to 15 (or 10) via /etc/default/monsterbox-cam and remove the tune-mjpg drop-in; delete the misleading -n comments so nobody 'fixes' latency by adding -n again. The real fix lives in the consumers (other surface): latest-frame-only relay in the Node proxies instead of pipe(), and CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1 / drain-loop in motion_tracking_service.py — flagged for the synthesizer, not actioned here.

findings.title: (b) Device-level stacking with OpenCV: motion_tracking_service.py opens /dev/videoN directly while mjpg-streamer (with 3 restarters behind it) holds it — one UVC STREAMON wins, tracker loses, matching 'motion tracking stopped working'
findings.evidence: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:342 (self.cap = cv2.VideoCapture(device_id)) with default --device /dev/video0 at :959, used whenever --stream-url is absent (:330-334 prefers the stream only if given). Every mjpg-streamer unit variant targets the same device and is backed by Restart=always plus two watchdogs, so after any contention race the streamer ALWAYS reacquires the camera and the tracker permanently loses. docs/development/BENCH-HANDOFF-2026-08-23.md:26-28 explicitly names this on sirdragomir ('check whether mjpg-streamer holds /dev/video0 exclusively while the tracker tries to open the device instead of the stream — the 5-second-lag fix and this may be one problem'). Conversely, if the tracker grabs the device first, install.sh's unit crash-loops at RestartSec=2 (install.sh:332-333) — fork/exec + failed V4L2 init every ~2-3s indefinitely, journal spam included; precedent of 42+ restarts documented at mjpg-launcher.sh:4-9.
findings.estimatedCost: Tracker-loses case: motion tracking simply dead (CPU freed, feature broken). Streamer-loses case: ~1-3% CPU of continuous fork/exec churn + journald writes to SD + watchdog restarts layered on top. Either way one of the two flagship camera features is down at all times by construction.
findings.fix: Make the tracker consume the MJPEG stream (--stream-url http://127.0.0.1:8090/?action=stream) as the DEFAULT and treat direct device open as an explicit opt-in only valid when mjpg-streamer is stopped; or gate tracker startup on 'is mjpg-streamer active' and refuse the device path with a named error. Single-consumer-of-the-device must be an enforced invariant, not luck.

findings.title: (b) Two independent drop-in writers can coexist and silently rule the service: tune-mjpg.sh's 20-monsterbox-vid.conf and webcamController's override.conf — editing the unit file or launcher then changes nothing
findings.evidence: scripts/tune-mjpg.sh:19-27 writes /etc/systemd/system/mjpg-streamer.service.d/20-monsterbox-vid.conf; controllers/webcamController.js:737-752 (applyDeviceToService) writes override.conf in the same directory with part-config geometry defaulting to q85 (:735) and a bare devicePath defaulting to /dev/video0 (:730), then daemon-reloads and restarts (:774-775). systemd applies drop-ins in lexical order, so override.conf's ExecStart reset beats 20-monsterbox-vid.conf, which beats the unit file, which beats scripts/mjpg-launcher.sh — four layers deep. The v11 audit (docs/evidence/v11-audit-2026-08-21/v11-uptime-perf.md:9-26) already called the applyDeviceToService writer a show-stopper; it remains in the code. On a node where the app runs as root (install.sh unit uses User=root for mjpg; if node itself runs privileged) one UI click permanently detaches the node from the git-tracked launcher config.
findings.estimatedCost: Zero steady-state CPU — the cost is diagnostic: hours of chasing 'I changed the config and nothing happened', plus the latent crash-loop when the hardcoded /dev/video0 goes stale after a USB blip (documented 42-restart precedent). On sirdragomir this is the first thing to audit: `systemctl cat mjpg-streamer` shows every layer in one output.
findings.fix: Rewrite applyDeviceToService to emit /etc/default/monsterbox-cam key=value lines (the launcher already sources it, mjpg-launcher.sh:16) and never ExecStart=; delete tune-mjpg.sh; add a boot-time or health-check warning when any mjpg-streamer.service.d drop-in overrides ExecStart.

findings.title: (d) Restart-time dead air is built in: ExecStartPre sleeps of 3-5s on units that restart frequently, multiplying every churn event into visible multi-second freezes
findings.evidence: scripts/mjpg-streamer.service:12 (ExecStartPre=/bin/sleep 3), install-mjpg-streamer-integration.sh:78 and setup-mjpg-streamer-service.sh:64 (ExecStartPre=/bin/sleep 5), start-mjpg-auto.sh:5 (sleep 3 inside the script). Combined with the restart machinery above (WatchdogSec 30s kills, watchdog-pair restarts, RestartSec 2-10), each restart is 5-10s of no frames. A browser on an MJPEG stream shows the LAST received frame during the gap, then jumps — indistinguishable to an operator from 'the video is N seconds behind'.
findings.estimatedCost: No CPU; pure availability/latency. In the WatchdogSec=30 scenario the sleeps alone are ~10-25% of the service's wall-clock lifetime.
findings.fix: The sleeps exist to wait for camera init; the by-id launcher makes them mostly unnecessary (device path is resolved fresh each start). Cut to sleep 1 or remove, and rely on Restart=on-failure + RestartSec for genuine not-ready cases.

reports.topSuspects: Ranked for the 5s lag + general slowness, from this surface: (1) NO FRAME-DROPPING DOWNSTREAM OF output_http — mjpg-streamer itself drops frames per client (intrinsic latency ~0.1-0.4s), but once frames enter the TCP connection to the Node same-origin proxy (webcamController.js:602/676 pipe with backpressure) or an in-order OpenCV stream reader, nothing drops: Linux TCP rmem autotuning stores multi-MB ≈ 100-200 frames ≈ 4-8s at the 24fps/q80 the tune-mjpg drop-in imposes (install.sh:412 → tune-mjpg.sh:26). The math lands almost exactly on the observed 5s. mjpg-side mitigation: restore 15fps (or 10) via /etc/default/monsterbox-cam and delete the drop-in; real fix is drop-latest relaying in the consumers. (2) RESTART CHURN — depending on which of the FIVE unit writers last ran on sirdragomir, the installed unit either SIGABRTs every 30s (WatchdogSec=30 on a non-sd_notify binary, scripts/mjpg-streamer.service:21, installed by install-webcam-watchdog.sh:18) or gets killed every 90s (Type=forking without -b, setup-webcam.sh:130 unit); layered on TWO uncoordinated snapshot watchdogs (timer every 30s + webcam-watchdog loop every 30s) that restart the service independently. Result: recurring 5-10s frame gaps (ExecStartPre sleeps + camera re-init) that present as frozen/lagging video, plus journal spam to SD. One command decides it: `systemctl show mjpg-streamer -p NRestarts` + `systemctl cat mjpg-streamer`. (3) DEVICE CONTENTION — motion_tracking_service.py:342 opens /dev/video0 directly while every mjpg-streamer variant claims the same device with Restart=always behind it; UVC allows one STREAMON, the streamer always re-wins, so the tracker dies (the 'OpenCV stopped working' symptom, corroborated by BENCH-HANDOFF-2026-08-23.md:26-28); in the reverse race install.sh's RestartSec=2 unit crash-loops every ~2-3s burning 1-3% CPU and SD writes indefinitely. (4) POSSIBLE SILENT YUYV FALLBACK — no config passes -y, but the jacksonliam experimental build all installers compile falls back to YUYV + software JPEG encode when the camera lacks MJPEG at the requested mode: 20-60% of a core and added per-frame encode latency; check `top` on mjpg_streamer (healthy MJPEG passthrough is ~0.1%, Orlok-measured). General 'whole machine slow' contribution from this surface is dominated by (2)+(3) churn and any (4) encode; a single healthy passthrough streamer is nearly free.

reports.surface: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py (OpenCV motion/person tracker), spawned exclusively by controllers/motionTrackingController.js startMotionTrackingProcess() with BOTH --device and --stream-url http://localhost:8090/?action=stream (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:32,380-402). Default detectionMode is 'person' (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:49).
reports.topSuspects: RANKED: (1) In 'person' mode the tracker runs HOG detectMultiScale on EVERY frame whenever no person is currently tracked (scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:525 — run_full_detect is forced true while cv_tracker_ok is false, which is the steady state at an empty bench). OpenCV HOG parallelizes across pyramid levels, so this pins up to all 4 Cortex-A72 cores at ~200-600ms per call, continuously. This alone explains 'whole machine is slow', and by starving mjpg-streamer's capture/encode threads and node it plausibly explains the operator-visible 5s MJPEG preview lag machine-wide. (2) The tracker consumes the MJPEG stream slower than mjpg-streamer produces it and its keep-latest frame-drop only operates WITHIN one 32KB socket read (py:393,403-413) — frames are 30-80KB, so at most one complete JPEG ever appears per read and nothing is dropped; the multi-second backlog lives in the loopback TCP send+recv buffers (kernel-bounded, ~1-4MB ≈ 25-100 frames), which at an effective 1.5-6 fps consumption rate is 5-20 seconds of latency. The tracker therefore acts on positions ~5s stale — head tracking chases where the person WAS, reading as 'motion tracking stopped working'. Note: this backlog is tracker-local (mjpg-streamer serves each HTTP client from its own thread), so it does not directly delay the browser preview; the preview lag is CPU starvation from (1) and/or a similar no-drop buffer in whatever proxies the preview (outside this surface — check the Node MJPEG proxy). (3) Every frame in 'person' mode ALSO pays the full unused background-subtraction pipeline: JPEG decode + grayscale + Gaussian blur + MOG2.apply + threshold + 5x5 open + 9x9 dilate x2 + 9x9 close (py:487-515), ~55-95ms/frame of pure waste, dragging even KCF-tracking frames to ~8-11fps ceiling and guaranteeing the consumer never catches up. (4) 'Stopped working' has silent failure paths: initialize() returns True even when the stream never connected (py:329-333), so the process reports initialized and then spins at 100Hz returning None forever with up to 30s reconnect backoff (py:383-391), while Node keeps serving the last-known-good status (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:415-416 only updates on output).

findings.title: (a) Captures from HTTP MJPEG stream, not the device; frame-dropping exists but is structurally defeated — backlog accumulates in kernel TCP buffers
findings.evidence: controllers/motionTrackingController.js:32,384-385 always pass --stream-url http://localhost:8090/?action=stream; scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:329-333 prefer the stream whenever stream_url is set (so the --device arg is dead in practice). Read path: py:393 reads exactly ONE 32KB chunk per process_frame call; py:403-413 parse all complete JPEGs in the local buffer and keep only the last one; py:415-416 cap the local buffer at 512KB. But a 640x480 MJPEG frame is 30-80KB (>32KB), so a single read almost never contains more than one complete frame — the keep-latest logic drops nothing, and the tracker walks the backlog strictly in order. The real queue is the loopback TCP send+recv buffers between mjpg-streamer and urllib (unbounded by this code, bounded only by kernel autotuning, ~1-4MB combined).
findings.estimatedCost: Latency, not memory: at 40KB/frame, 1-4MB of kernel buffer holds 25-100 stale frames; consumed at the tracker's effective 1.5-6 fps that is a stable 5-20s pipeline delay — matching the observed ~5s. Python-side memory is bounded (512KB cap py:415, 30-entry frame_times py:798). mjpg-streamer skips frames for blocked clients, so the backlog plateaus rather than grows.
findings.fix: Drain-then-process: per loop, read the socket non-blocking (or in a reader thread) until EAGAIN, decode ONLY the newest complete JPEG, discard the rest. Minimal same-shape change: loop stream_conn.read(32768) until the buffer holds at least one complete frame AND a subsequent short read indicates the socket is drained, then process the last frame found. Also shrink the kernel view of the queue by setting a small SO_RCVBUF (e.g. 64KB) on the stream socket so backpressure pushes drops into mjpg-streamer instead of into latency.

findings.title: (b) 'person' mode = HOG+SVM pedestrian detector at 400px width, scale 1.05, winStride 8x8 — ~200-600ms per call, parallelized across all cores
findings.evidence: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:136-144 (cv2.HOGDescriptor + default people detector, 64x128 window), py:168-182 (_detect_persons_hog resizes to 400px wide, detectMultiScale winStride=(8,8), padding=(4,4), scale=1.05). At 400x300 and scale 1.05 that is ~17 pyramid levels. Nominally run every detect_interval=5 frames with KCF in between (py:77, controllers/motionTrackingController.js:48), plus KCF re-init on every detection cycle (py:661-665).
findings.estimatedCost: On a Pi 4B: ~0.8-2 core-seconds per detectMultiScale call; OpenCV parallel_for spreads it over up to 4 threads, so ~200-600ms wall per call with ALL cores busy. Per-frame fixed overhead on top: JPEG decode ~15-25ms (py:419-420), gray+blur ~5-8ms, MOG2+morphology ~40-70ms (py:495-515), KCF update ~10-40ms (py:268). Net throughput: ~3-6 fps with a person tracked, ~1.5-3 fps with none.
findings.fix: Replace HOG with the MOG2 motion pipeline it already computes (motion mode is ~10x cheaper and adequate for 'is someone there + where'), or if person classification must stay, run HOG at most 1-2x/second on a timer, at 320px width, and only on frames where the (already-computed) foreground mask shows activity.

findings.title: (b/prime CPU sink) HOG runs EVERY frame, not every 5th, whenever no target is tracked — the steady state at an idle bench
findings.evidence: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:525: run_full_detect = (frames_since_detect >= detect_interval) OR NOT self.cv_tracker_ok. cv_tracker_ok starts False (py:76) and stays False until a person is detected (py:661-665) — so with nobody in frame, full HOG detection runs on every single assembled frame, back to back, forever. py:543 also forces full detection the frame after any KCF loss.
findings.estimatedCost: Continuous ~150-350% CPU (of 400%) on a Pi 4B doing nothing useful, 24/7 while tracking is enabled and the room is empty. This is the single largest design-level CPU sink on the node and starves mjpg-streamer, node server.js, the jaw/servo daemon and the audio monitor — the 'whole machine is SLOW' symptom, and indirectly the preview lag.
findings.fix: Rate-limit detection by TIME, not frames: e.g. if not cv_tracker_ok, still require (now - last_detect_time) >= 0.5s before running HOG. One clock check at py:525.

findings.title: Unconditional background-subtraction + morphology pipeline runs every frame even in 'person' mode where its output is never read
findings.evidence: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:487-515: cvtColor, GaussianBlur(5x5), bg_subtractor.apply (MOG2, history 500), threshold, MORPH_OPEN (5x5 ellipse), dilate(9x9 ellipse, iterations=2), MORPH_CLOSE(9x9) execute before any mode check. fg_mask is only consumed in 'motion'/'all'/'person+motion' modes (py:550-551,650) — in the default 'person' mode (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:49) it is 100% waste, including on the cheap KCF-only frames (py:531-543) that were designed to be fast.
findings.estimatedCost: ~40-70ms/frame at 640x480 on a Pi 4B (MOG2 ~15-25ms, dilate x2 9x9 ~10-15ms, close ~8ms, open ~5ms, blur ~4ms) ≈ 15-40% of one core at the achievable frame rates; caps even tracker-mode frames at ~8-11fps, ensuring the consumer stays slower than the 15-30fps producer (feeds finding (a)).
findings.fix: Hoist the mode check: compute fg_mask only when mode in ('motion','all','person+motion') or on the fallback path. Pure code motion of py:489-515 into the branch at py:550.

findings.title: (c) No processing frame-rate cap and no stale-frame pacing — only the JSON output is throttled
findings.evidence: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:925 time.sleep(0.01) per loop iteration is the only pacing (also caps ingest at one 32KB chunk per ≥10ms, ~2 iterations per frame). py:900-901,920-923: output_interval = 1/25s throttles printing only; every assembled frame is fully processed regardless. Camera FPS is set to 15 only on the dead device path (py:350); the stream path has no rate control at all.
findings.estimatedCost: Zero direct cost, but it means the tracker's CPU consumption is 'whatever the pipeline costs x every frame the stream delivers' with no ceiling, and there is no mechanism to skip ahead when behind. Combined with (a) it converts overload into latency instead of into dropped frames.
findings.fix: Target processing rate explicitly (e.g. 10fps): after assembling the newest frame, skip processing if now - last_processed < 0.1s; always keep draining the socket regardless (see finding a).

findings.title: (d) When it can't keep up: latency plateaus (5-20s stale positions), no memory growth, no crash — plus three silent-death modes that read as 'stopped working'
findings.evidence: Bounded memory: py:415-416 (512KB buffer cap), py:797-799 (frame_times capped at 30), py:718 (tracked_objects pruned). So overload manifests purely as stale target_position — head tracking commands aim seconds behind reality and the 0.5s persistence window (py:96,789) plus EMA smoothing (py:772-774) mask the staleness. Silent-death modes: (1) py:329-333 initialize() returns True even when _connect_stream() failed, and py:904-911 prints initialized:true immediately — Node resolves the start as successful (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:421-424) while zero frames flow; the loop then spins at 100Hz with reconnect backoff to 30s (py:383-391) and never emits another status, and Node's trackingStatus keeps the stale entry forever. (2) Node kills the process at a 10s init timeout (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:469-475) — a cold stream connect (3s timeout, py:368) plus first HOG pass can plausibly overrun it under load. (3) Unexpected exits do leave a tombstone now (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:444-466), so a true crash is at least visible in .err.
findings.estimatedCost: Not a resource cost — a correctness cliff: at ~5s staleness the servo tracks empty space, and in scan mode re-commands the pan servo continuously. Diagnosis cost is high because every status field ('active: true', fps, positions) looks healthy while describing the past.
findings.fix: Two small changes: make initialize() return False (or emit initialized:false) when the stream connect fails so Node's start call fails loudly; and include a staleness metric in the status JSON — e.g. bytes currently unread / frames discarded — or compare mjpg-streamer's frame timestamp header if available, so Node can flag 'tracker is N seconds behind'.

findings.title: (e) No /dev/video0 conflict: the tracker never opens the device in practice — but it also never falls back to it
findings.evidence: controllers/motionTrackingController.js:384-385 always passes --stream-url, and scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:329-333 takes the stream branch unconditionally when stream_url is set, returning before cv2.VideoCapture is ever constructed (py:335-353). mjpg-streamer keeps sole ownership of /dev/video0. Conversely, if mjpg-streamer is down, the tracker does NOT fall back to the device — it just reconnect-loops (py:383-391).
findings.estimatedCost: No contention cost. The dependency does mean tracker health is transitively mjpg-streamer health, and a preview consumer + tracker both pull separate full MJPEG streams from mjpg-streamer (~600KB/s each over loopback — negligible bandwidth, but each client costs mjpg-streamer a send thread).
findings.fix: None needed for exclusivity. Optionally fall back to cv2.VideoCapture when the stream stays unreachable for >30s — but only if mjpg-streamer is confirmed dead, otherwise the fallback itself would create the device conflict.

findings.title: Per-status-line fan-out in Node: maybeDriveHead runs at up to 25Hz off tracker stdout, and Python INFO logs stream into monsterbox.err via console.warn
findings.evidence: controllers/motionTrackingController.js:409-419: every stdout JSON line (emitted at up to 25Hz, py:900-901) triggers maybeDriveHead — async, with awaited readConfig/calibration-store reads on the claim/guardrail paths (60s cache at controllers/motionTrackingController.js:633-634 blunts most of it, and the 50ms min-interval at :763 bounds servo commands to 20Hz). Separately, Python logging goes to stderr (py:24) and every stderr chunk is console.warn'd (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:433-435) → /var/log/monsterbox.err on SD; 'KCF tracker initialized on bbox ...' (py:254) fires on EVERY re-detection cycle — with a person present at ~5fps/detect_interval=5 that is ~1 SD-card log write per second, indefinitely.
findings.estimatedCost: Node-side: low single-digit % CPU at 25Hz (JSON.parse + map writes + mostly-cached async chain) — real but minor. SD writes: ~1 line/s ≈ 86K lines/day of .err churn on a platform whose CLAUDE.md mandates minimizing SD writes; also buries real errors in .err.
findings.fix: Demote py:254 (and the per-mode-change chatter) to logging.debug, or log KCF re-init only when the bbox changed materially; in Node, forward Python stderr lines matching WARNING/ERROR only.

findings.title: KCF tracker is destroyed and re-created from scratch on every full-detection cycle instead of being re-seeded only on drift
findings.evidence: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:661-665: after every run_full_detect pass with any detection, _init_cv_tracker() constructs a new cv2.TrackerKCF and re-inits it — every 5th frame in the best case. KCF init recomputes the full correlation-filter model, costlier than an update.
findings.estimatedCost: ~20-60ms extra every 5th frame on a Pi 4B (roughly doubles the tracking-mode overhead vs. update-only). Second-order next to HOG, but it erodes the entire benefit the detect_interval/tracker design was meant to buy.
findings.fix: Only re-init when the new detection's bbox IoU with cv_tracker_bbox is below ~0.5 (i.e. tracker actually drifted); otherwise keep the live tracker.

reports.surface: Node-side video/streaming paths: calibration webcam proxy (routes/setup/calibration.js -> controllers/webcamController.js streamMJPEG), orchestration MJPEG proxy (routes/api/orchestrationRoutes.js), stream-embedding pages (views/setup/calibration.ejs, public/js/dashboard.js, views/orchestration/index.ejs Fleet Command Center, public/js/head-animation.js), the OpenCV tracker child (controllers/motionTrackingController.js + scripts/motion_tracking_service.py), and the per-request Express middleware those pages' pollers hammer (server.js).
reports.topSuspects: RANKED. (1) THE DEPLOY GAP IS THE 5-SECOND LAG: the repo HEAD (commit 3aba5df, 2026-08-23) contains a bench-measured fix whose commit message IS the diagnosis for sirdragomir: motion_tracking_service.py measured at ~200% CPU (2 of 4 cores) running HOG person-detection at 400px/1.05 pyramid on every frame, at nice -5 INHERITED from the monsterbox.service priority drop-in (scripts/optimize-pi-performance.sh:51), legally starving node server, servo daemon and the video proxy; simultaneously its MJPEG reader pulled only 32KB per processing cycle (< the ~0.45 MB/s the stream produces) so frames aged in the kernel socket buffer and 'latest' was seconds old — the exact ~5s-behind preview. mjpg-streamer itself measured 0.8% (camera outputs native MJPG). The fix (os.nice(15), drain-to-latest bounded 4MB, 10fps processing cap, HOG 320px/1.1) exists ONLY at HEAD; docs/development/BENCH-HANDOFF-2026-08-23.md:43 records the node at f068e270, which PREDATES both 3aba5df and 8e5ad77 — code travels by rsync deploy, so the node almost certainly still runs the pre-fix tracker. (2) 'OpenCV stopped working' is the pre-8e5ad77 silent-death/silent-clobber behavior (unexpected tracker exit deleted all state; enabling head tracking silently restarted the pipeline under a motion session) — the mutual-exclusion + tombstone fix is also undeployed; secondary possibility named in the handoff: tracker falling back to opening /dev/video0 directly while mjpg-streamer holds it. (3) GENERAL SLOWNESS is the tracker's 2 cores at elevated priority PLUS an accumulation of Node-side per-client duplication and pollers: every stream viewer is its own full proxy chain with software TLS on a CPU with no crypto extensions (FCC = 1 stream per online node per open page, double-proxied through two Node processes), phantom streams from background dashboard/calibration tabs and 'Open Stream' tabs that nothing ever closes, 100ms status pollers on calibration/head-animation pages, a VU meter that drives ~2 full Python+ALSA interpreter spawns per second while a mic part is selected, and a global Express middleware that does 2 disk reads + 2 JSON.parses on every one of those requests. None of the proxies drops frames (byte-faithful pipe), so any CPU stall converts kernel-socket backlog into standing video latency that never drains.

findings.title: Undeployed tracker fix: HOG at ~2 cores at nice -5 + 32KB/cycle stream reads = the measured 5s lag (design flaw live on node)
findings.evidence: Commit 3aba5df message (git show 3aba5df): 'Bench measurement on sirdragomir: motion_tracking_service.py at ~200% CPU... at nice -5 INHERITED... the operator's preview ran ~5 seconds behind reality. mjpg-streamer measured 0.8%'. Pre-fix design visible in the diff: scripts/motion_tracking_service.py old _read_mjpeg_frame read one 32KB chunk per cycle (fixed drain-loop now at :422-432), old HOG at 400px/scale 1.05 (now :174-188), no processing cap (now :947-949, 10fps), no self-deprioritization (now :1047-1051 os.nice(15)). Node runs f068e270 per docs/development/BENCH-HANDOFF-2026-08-23.md:43 ('node = f068e270'), which predates 3aba5df — deploys are rsync (monsterbox-fleet), so HEAD's fixes are not on the box.
findings.estimatedCost: ~200% CPU (2 of 4 Cortex-A72 cores) at nice -5, bench-measured; kernel-socket frame aging producing ~5s of standing video latency; head tracking chasing 5s-old positions; everything else on the box (Express, servo daemon, proxies) starved at lower priority.
findings.fix: Deploy HEAD (>= 3aba5df and 8e5ad77) to sirdragomir via the rsync deploy, restart monsterbox.service, kill any running motion_tracking_service.py, then verify on-node per fleet-verify (grep for 'max_process_fps' in scripts/motion_tracking_service.py and 'headTrackingShutDown' in controllers/motionTrackingController.js).

findings.title: systemd Nice=-5 drop-in is inherited by every child_process — any CPU-hungry child legally starves the server and stream
findings.evidence: scripts/optimize-pi-performance.sh:49-57 writes /etc/systemd/system/monsterbox.service.d/10-priority.conf with Nice=-5, CPUWeight=90; children spawned by Node (python3 tracker at controllers/motionTrackingController.js:402, servo daemon, mpg123, wrappers) inherit that niceness. Confirmed as the amplifier in commit 3aba5df's message ('detection legally outranked the server, the servo daemon and the video stream'). Only the tracker self-demotes (motion_tracking_service.py:1047-1051) — every other child still runs at -5.
findings.estimatedCost: Zero when children are idle; priority inversion whenever any child burns CPU — converts a 1-core child bug into whole-machine slowness because the scheduler prefers the child over Express/the servo daemon at equal weight.
findings.fix: Spawn long-running analysis children with explicit deprioritization from Node (spawn option or nice wrapper) rather than relying on each script to call os.nice; or split the drop-in so only the server process (not children) gets the boost (systemd can't do per-child, so the spawn-side fix is the real one).

findings.title: (a) Per-client upstream duplication: every browser viewer opens its own connection through the full proxy chain; FCC opens one per online node automatically
findings.evidence: controllers/webcamController.js:602 (new nodeFetch to http://127.0.0.1:8090/?action=stream per request; route wired at routes/setup/calibration.js:1499). Orchestration proxy routes/api/orchestrationRoutes.js:618-676 opens a fresh axios stream per viewer, and its upstream is the TARGET NODE'S EXPRESS PROXY, not mjpg-streamer: routes/conversation.js:101,106 return /setup/calibration/api/webcam/parts/:id/stream. Chain per FCC viewer per node: mjpg-streamer -> node Express (TLS encrypt, :3000) -> orchestrator Express (TLS decrypt + re-encrypt) -> browser. views/orchestration/index.ejs:298 auto-starts a stream for EVERY online node card on page load; :465 starts a SECOND stream of the same node for the zoom modal while the card stream keeps running.
findings.estimatedCost: Capture/encode is 1x regardless (camera native MJPG; mjpg-streamer bench-measured 0.8%). Per viewer: ~0.3-0.6 MB/s copied through 1-2 Node event loops plus software TLS per hop (BCM2711 has no ARMv8 crypto extensions) — roughly 2-6% of a core per viewer per Node hop, doubling on the double-proxied FCC path; per-chunk event-loop wakeups compete with everything else in each Node process. 3 FCC pages open = 3 full chains PER NODE.
findings.fix: Fan-out in the node proxy: one upstream connection to mjpg-streamer shared by all local viewers (a latest-frame broadcaster keyed by part id); have the orchestrator proxy hit the node's :8090 output (or the node proxy) once and fan out likewise. Smallest change: single shared upstream in webcamController.streamMJPEG with per-client writers.

findings.title: (b) No frame-dropping anywhere in the proxy chain — byte-faithful pipe() turns any stall into permanent standing latency
findings.evidence: controllers/webcamController.js:676 'nodeReadable.pipe(res)' and routes/api/orchestrationRoutes.js:676 'response.data.pipe(res)' — neither parses MJPEG boundaries or discards stale frames. No unbounded in-process Buffer (pipe backpressure is intact), but the backlog lives in kernel socket buffers at each hop (upstream loopback rcvbuf + TLS sendbuf, then repeat at the orchestrator hop). mjpg-streamer only skips frames for a client once its send() blocks — i.e., after every downstream buffer is FULL, and that full pipeline IS the standing delay; MJPEG has no timestamps so the browser renders backlog in order, forever behind.
findings.estimatedCost: At 640x480 q60 @15fps (~0.45 MB/s): each hop's socket buffers can hold ~0.5-2s of video; the FCC double-proxy path stacks 3 TCP connections (6 buffer sides) — several seconds of latency that accrues during any CPU stall (e.g. the tracker eating 2 cores) and NEVER drains afterward. This is the mechanism that converts finding #1's CPU starvation into the visible 5s lag.
findings.fix: Boundary-aware relay: in streamMJPEG, parse the multipart boundary and, when res.write() reports backpressure, drop to the newest complete JPEG instead of pausing the upstream (latest-frame semantics). Bonus: explicitly shrink socket buffers on both sockets to bound worst-case backlog.

findings.title: (c) Phantom streams: background dashboard tabs, hidden calibration tab-panes, 'Open Stream' tabs, and per-node FCC cards all hold MJPEG connections indefinitely
findings.evidence: public/js/dashboard.js:1281-1310 loads the stream on every dashboard load (call sites :640, :682) — zero document.hidden/visibilitychange handling anywhere in dashboard.js (grep confirms only pollers guard hidden, the img never pauses). views/setup/calibration.ejs:3417 camPreview starts streaming the moment a webcam part is selected and keeps streaming while the operator works in other Bootstrap tab-panes (display toggling only; no shown/hidden.bs.tab teardown exists — grep at :559-571 shows plain tabs). :3424 'Open Stream' target=_blank creates a raw stream client no page logic can ever stop. :2512-2522 the Advanced tab adds a SECOND stream (advStreamImg) while camPreview persists, and the Python tracker is a third mjpg-streamer client. views/orchestration/index.ejs:298 one stream per online node with no visibility pause; :421-426 auto-restarts any dead stream every 15s poll (good for recovery, also guarantees background tabs re-latch).
findings.estimatedCost: Each phantom = one full proxy chain from finding (a): ~0.45 MB/s + TLS + event-loop load, 24/7. An operator with a dashboard tab, a calibration tab (2 streams), and an FCC tab (N nodes) in a background window quietly holds 3+N chains against a 4-core box.
findings.fix: visibilitychange handler on every stream-embedding page: clear img.src on hidden, restore on visible (dashboard.js, calibration.ejs, orchestration/index.ejs); tear down camPreview/advStreamImg on Bootstrap hidden.bs.tab; consider a server-side idle cap (max concurrent proxy clients per part, oldest dropped).

findings.title: (d) 100ms status pollers on calibration and head-animation pages (10 req/s each over HTTPS)
findings.evidence: views/setup/calibration.ejs:2674-2697 setInterval 100ms polling /setup/calibration/api/webcam/motion-tracking/status (busy-flag + document.hidden guards present). public/js/head-animation.js:720-726 identical 100ms poll of /setup/head-animation/api/head-tracking/:id/status. Server handler is a cheap in-memory Map read (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:234-262), so the cost is per-request overhead: TLS record + Express routing + the global middleware below.
findings.estimatedCost: ~10 HTTPS req/s per open page while tracking is active; with the per-request middleware (next finding) each request adds 2 file reads + 2 JSON.parses — order 3-8% of a core per page on a Pi 4B, worse while the box is already contended.
findings.fix: Poll at 250-300ms (overlay is drawn from 10fps tracker output anyway — 100ms gains nothing), or push status over the existing response of the stream page via long-poll; keep the busy/hidden guards.

findings.title: VU meter poll spawns a full Python+ALSA interpreter ~2x/second while a mic part is selected on the calibration page
findings.evidence: views/setup/calibration.ejs:3360 setInterval(updateCalMicVU, 150) fetching /setup/audio/api/audio-levels; routes/setup/audio.js:580-639 runs microphone_cli.py per probe with only a 500ms cache TTL (audio.js:563) and in-flight coalescing; calibration.ejs:2836-2843 comment documents each spawn as 'a fresh Python interpreter that has to initialise ALSA (~350ms, 6.5KB of stderr)'. The historic interval-stacking leak (multiple VU loops after part switches) is fixed at :2844-2847 — but only in repo code, subject to the same deploy gap as finding #1.
findings.estimatedCost: ~2 interpreter spawns/sec sustained = roughly 30-70% of one core while the mic panel is open (interpreter start + PyAudio/ALSA init + 100ms capture each), plus fork/exec pressure. On the pre-fix node code the stacking bug multiplies this per part-switch — matching 'the whole machine got progressively slower'.
findings.fix: Replace spawn-per-sample with one persistent level-meter child (like the tracker: long-lived process emitting levels on stdout), or raise CACHE_TTL/poll to 500ms-1s; deploy the stacking fix.

findings.title: Global per-request middleware does 2 disk reads + 2 JSON.parses on EVERY request, including all poller traffic
findings.evidence: server.js:403-447: every request calls loadConfig() (uncached fs.readFile + JSON.parse of config/app-config.json, server.js:802-807) then fs.readFile of data/characters.json + JSON.parse (:422-424). services/configService.js:12-19 readConfig is likewise uncached for all other callers. Poller load from findings above funnels through this: 10/s tracking status + ~7/s VU + dashboard 1s/1s/3s pollers.
findings.estimatedCost: 20-40 file reads + JSON.parses/sec under one open calibration page (page-cached so no SD wear on reads, ~0.5-1ms each) — order 2-4% of a core plus GC churn; adds tail latency to every request on a contended box.
findings.fix: Cache both files in-process with an mtime check or 1-2s TTL (selectedCharacter is already authoritative in memory per the comment at :405-407, so the disk read is only for theme-like fields).

findings.title: Head-tracking drive path logs to SD at up to 20 lines/sec while active
findings.evidence: controllers/motionTrackingController.js:903 console.log('Head tracking (positional): ...') and :863 (continuous variant) execute on every servo command; rate floor is minIntervalMs=50 at :763 (up to 20 Hz). Logs go to /var/log/monsterbox.log (systemd append). Prior incident at :686-688: 10,409 identical lines in one night. CLAUDE.md mandates minimizing SD writes.
findings.estimatedCost: Low CPU (<1%), but a sustained 20 lines/sec write stream to SD card while tracking runs — SD wear + log noise; contributes to I/O contention during shows.
findings.fix: Demote the per-command line to a debug flag or sample it (log 1-in-50 / on state change only).

findings.title: Per-stream-start health check fetches a full snapshot (extra frame grab + buffer) before every proxy connect
findings.evidence: controllers/webcamController.js:562 streamMJPEG calls checkMjpgStreamerHealth() -> probeMjpgStreamer (:327-368) which GETs the mjpg-streamer root AND a full ?action=snapshot (buffered via arrayBuffer at :351) before connecting; plus a 2-attempt retry loop with 1s sleeps at :595-621. FCC auto-reconnect (orchestration/index.ejs:421-426) re-triggers this every 15s for any dead camera.
findings.estimatedCost: One ~20-40KB snapshot fetch + buffer per stream (re)connect; trivial steady-state, but adds ~100-300ms connect latency per viewer and multiplies under FCC auto-retry when a camera is flapping.
findings.fix: Skip the probe on the stream path (the connect itself fails fast with the 5s AbortController at :598-600) or cache the health verdict for a few seconds.

findings.title: _activeVideoUse device-usage tracking is wrong under concurrent viewers (reporting only, no perf cost)
findings.evidence: controllers/webcamController.js:637-643 sets a single Map entry keyed by devicePath for every stream client (:709 Map declaration); :654 the FIRST client to disconnect deletes the entry while other clients still stream, so probeDevices/devicesInUse (:198-199, :95-102) report the device free while N-1 proxies still run.
findings.estimatedCost: No CPU cost; misleads diagnosis of 'who holds the camera' — relevant because the handoff's OpenCV theory involves device contention.
findings.fix: Reference-count per devicePath (increment on connect, decrement on cleanup, delete at zero).

findings.title: Undeployed 'one camera consumer' + tombstone fix means the live node still loses OpenCV tracking silently
findings.evidence: controllers/motionTrackingController.js:90-96 (motion start shuts down head tracking, logged), :444-466 (unexpected exit logs to .err with exit code and leaves tombstone status), :957-959 (head-tracking takeover logged) — all landed in 8e5ad77, which postdates the node's f068e270 (docs/development/BENCH-HANDOFF-2026-08-23.md:20-28,43). Pre-fix behavior: tracker death deleted ALL state so status reported nothing had ever run, and feature toggles silently clobbered each other — the exact 'OpenCV was working and just stopped' report. Handoff :26-28 also flags the device-vs-stream contention theory (tracker opening /dev/video0 while mjpg-streamer holds it — fallback path at scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:341-365 only runs when --stream-url is absent; controller always passes it at controllers/motionTrackingController.js:385, so contention requires the stream connect to fail).
findings.estimatedCost: Not a CPU cost — a diagnosability hole: on the live node an OpenCV death is invisible (empty status, no .err line), so the symptom is unresolvable there until the deploy lands.
findings.fix: Same deploy as finding #1; then read /var/log/monsterbox.err for 'EXITED unexpectedly (code N)' and GET /api/webcam/motion-tracking/status for the tombstone.

findings.title: Dashboard runs 4 concurrent network pollers plus the webcam stream on every open tab
findings.evidence: public/js/dashboard.js:408 pollActivity @1000ms (/conversation/api/lurk-mode/activity-status, no document.hidden guard), :1379 pollHeadTrackStatus @1000ms, :492 lurk motion @3000ms, :843 character-change @10000ms, :1937 console @3000ms; DOM-only timers :2303/:2312 @1500ms (cheap). Each network poll traverses the server.js:403 middleware (2 disk reads + parses).
findings.estimatedCost: ~2-3 HTTPS req/s per open dashboard (foreground or background — activity poll has no hidden guard), ~1-2% core each; additive per tab and on top of the tab's permanent MJPEG stream.
findings.fix: Add document.hidden guards to pollActivity/pollHeadTrackStatus (mirroring the calibration pollers), and pause the webcam img on visibilitychange.

reports.surface: BACKGROUND CPU on the node server (sirdragomir): server.js startup timers, AudioHealthMonitor, performance collector, node discovery, goblin reconnect, idle/random pose engine, jaw/speech tick loops, movement telemetry auto-flush, stall-guard sweep, liveness watchdog, plus the client-polling load these serve. Repo at /home/user/MonsterBox, HEAD 3aba5df.
reports.topSuspects: RANKED CAUSE OF 5s VIDEO LAG + GENERAL SLOWNESS: (1) The OpenCV tracker (scripts/motion_tracking_service.py) is the documented culprit for BOTH symptoms — the in-repo comments record the exact live failure: it inherits the monsterbox service's elevated nice -5 and was 'measured at the bench eating two of the Pi 4B's four cores while legally starving the server, the servo daemon and the video stream the operator was watching (~5 s behind reality)' (scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:1041-1046), and its old read path pulled only 32KB per processing cycle from mjpg-streamer while the stream produces ~15fps x ~40KB, so frames queued in the KERNEL socket buffer and the 'latest' frame was seconds old — 'the bench's 5-seconds-behind video' (scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:416-421). HEAD contains the fixes (drain-to-latest :422-432, max_process_fps=10 cap :946-949, os.nice(15) :1047-1050, CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1 :357-363) in commits 3aba5df/8e5ad77 — but MonsterBox code travels by rsync deploy, not git, so the FIRST verification step is proving the deployed tracker on sirdragomir actually contains 'max_process_fps' and 'os.nice(15)' (grep on-node); if not, the live node is still running the uncapped nice -5 tracker: ~2 cores of HOG person-detection (detection-mode default 'person', motionTrackingController.js:399; HOG detectMultiScale scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:183-187) + MOG2 per frame, which simultaneously explains lag, tracker 'stopped working' (starved/steward-killed), and whole-box slowness. (2) 'OpenCV tracking stopped' also matches the honest-death change in 8e5ad77: an unexpectedly-exited tracker now leaves a tombstone status instead of pretending (motionTrackingController.js:445-465) — check trackingStatus for exited:true and /var/log/monsterbox.err for the EXITED line. (3) No MJPEG frame-dropping anywhere in Node: both proxies are plain pipes (webcamController.js:676 nodeReadable.pipe(res); orchestrationRoutes.js:676 response.data.pipe(res)) with per-client upstream duplication (a new mjpg-streamer connection per viewer, and fleet views are double-hop node→node→streamer), so a slow/stalled browser accumulates latency in socket buffers indefinitely — a secondary, per-client lag source. (4) The Node server's own background timers total only ~1-3% of one core at idle and are NOT the slowness; the worst offenders if conditions degrade are: servo-daemon-down fallback (a python interpreter spawn per 80ms transition frame, 'seconds each on a Pi 4', hardwareService/index.js:788-791) and lurk watcher degraded mode (one python3 gpio_read.py spawn per second, lurkMotionWatcherService.js:262,279). (5) 'Audio Health Monitor started' appearing TWICE is one start printing two identical lines (AudioHealthMonitor.js:50 + server.js:933) — it CANNOT stack intervals (isMonitoring guard AudioHealthMonitor.js:34-37); a true double-start would print '⚠️ Audio Health Monitor already running' (:35). Growth-over-time: movement-telemetry flush cost grows to a ~1MB pretty-printed read+rewrite every 30s (cap 5000 entries), and perf history grows in RAM for 30 days; nothing else unbounded.

findings.title: (a) Timer inventory — every recurring timer in the node server, interval and per-tick cost
findings.evidence: 20ms servoCommandBuffer flush loop, on-demand+guarded (services/movement/servoCommandBuffer.js:222-246); 100ms speech co-expression tick during utterances (services/speechExpressionService.js:56,355); 200ms idle-liveliness head tick between turns (speechExpressionService.js:57,504); 250ms idle-loop micro-motion while a pose is held and microMovement.enabled (services/movement/idleLoopService.js:24,171-205); 5s perf console tick, cheap modulo — heavy work only every 12th tick = 60s: wpctl status spawn + mjpg health fetch (server.js:988-1015; services/pipewireService.js:667-670); 5s audio-level cache sweep, module-level, trivial (routes/setup/audio.js:571-578); 5s audioLoop monitor only while a loop plays (services/audioLoopService.js:35-44); 30s AudioHealthMonitor — one 'wpctl status' subprocess per tick (services/AudioHealthMonitor.js:17,46-48,80); 30s node-discovery avahi-browse subprocess (services/nodeDiscoveryService.js:27,186,314); 30s MemoryMonitor in-proc, negligible (services/resource/memoryMonitor.js:19,32); 30s movement-telemetry flush — full read+parse+pretty-stringify+rewrite of data/movement-telemetry.json when any motion happened (services/movement/movementTelemetry.js:13,52-100,175-181; started server.js:965-967); 30s goblin heartbeat+reconnect — HTTP dial w/ 5s timeout per offline goblin, forever unless expectedOffline (services/goblinManagerService.js:31,34,518-543,556-591); 30s stream-routing dead-stream sweep, in-proc (services/streamRoutingService.js:285-292, started at module load hardwareService/index.js:2052); 30s autoAI no-op tick per enabled animatronic (services/autoAIService.js:45-49); 60s STT session cleanup, in-proc (services/serverSTTListener.js:29-32); 60s EL WebSocket session cleanup (services/elevenLabsWebSocketService.js:256,395-398); 300s performance collector — 'top -bn1' + 'df' subprocesses + thermal sysfs, 1 SD write/hour (server.js:976; services/systemService.js:30-84,151-184); 300s stall-guard sweep — python3 servo_cli.py reconcile spawn (server.js:238; services/hardwareService/stallGuard.js:50-73,161-166); 1000ms lurk PIR poll ONLY in degraded mode — python3 spawn per tick (services/lurkMotionWatcherService.js:31,262,279); event-chained (not interval) idle pose loop: pose every 3-8s hold + 2s transition of up-to-64 80ms frames (idleLoopService.js:355-366,374-383; transitionEngine.js:96-99,511-519)
findings.estimatedCost: Idle node server total ≈1-3% of one A72 core, dominated by subprocess forks (wpctl 30s ~80-150ms CPU, avahi-browse 30s ~100-300ms, top/df 300s ~300-500ms, servo_cli reconcile 300s ~1-2.5s). In-proc ticks are microseconds each.
findings.fix: No single fix; see individual findings. The inventory is the deliverable for the synthesizer.

findings.title: (b) Audio Health Monitor 'started TWICE' is duplicate LOGGING, not a stacked interval
findings.evidence: AudioHealthMonitor.start() prints '🔊 Audio Health Monitor started (checking every 30s)' itself (services/AudioHealthMonitor.js:50, checkInterval=30000 at :17) AND server.js prints the byte-identical string right after calling it (server.js:932-933). start() is guarded: a second call prints '⚠️ Audio Health Monitor already running' and returns (AudioHealthMonitor.js:33-37); setCheckInterval() does stop()-then-start() safely (:250-254). Singleton export (:262).
findings.estimatedCost: Zero — one 30s interval exists. Each tick forks 'wpctl status' (~80-150ms CPU on Pi 4B) = ~0.4% of one core. Recovery path can restart wireplumber (audio hiccup, not CPU).
findings.fix: Delete the duplicate log line at server.js:933 (the monitor logs its own start). Grep the live log for 'already running' to prove no genuine double-start ever happened.

findings.title: (b) goblinManagerService.startHeartbeatMonitor CAN stack: no guard, handle never stored
findings.evidence: startHeartbeatMonitor() calls setInterval without checking for or storing an existing handle (services/goblinManagerService.js:556-591) — unlike every other loop in the codebase (cf. systemService.js:174, nodeDiscoveryService.js:311, servoCommandBuffer.js:210). It is currently called exactly once from the constructor (:34), so it does not stack today, but the timer can also never be stopped or unref'd.
findings.estimatedCost: Today: one 30s tick; CPU trivial, but attemptReconnectAll dials every offline non-expectedOffline goblin with a 5s-timeout fetch every 30s forever (:518-543) — network churn, and saveGoblins() SD writes on status flaps (:585).
findings.fix: Store the handle, guard 'if (this._hbTimer) return', add .unref(), and expose a stop() — 4 lines.

findings.title: (b) streamRoutingService.startPeriodicCleanup has no guard and no stored handle; started as a module-load side effect
findings.evidence: startPeriodicCleanup(intervalMs) is a bare setInterval with no dedup and no saved handle (services/streamRoutingService.js:285-292); it is invoked at import time of the hardware service (services/hardwareService/index.js:2052: 'streamRoutingService.startPeriodicCleanup(30000)'). ESM module caching means once per process today; any second call stacks forever.
findings.estimatedCost: Per tick: iterate tracked streams + process.kill(pid,0) — microseconds. Risk is structural (stacking/unstoppable), not current CPU.
findings.fix: Guard with a stored handle + unref, and move the call from module scope into server startup so tests importing hardwareService don't start it.

findings.title: (b) speechExpressionService.stopSpeaking overwrites s.settleTimer without clearing a running settle interval
findings.evidence: stopSpeaking creates a new 100ms settle interval and assigns s.settleTimer = settle without clearInterval on an existing one (services/speechExpressionService.js:446-454); startSpeaking DOES clear it (:342). Two stopSpeaking calls in quick succession (double stop events from the TTS pipeline) run two concurrent 10Hz intervals commanding the same head servo via jawServoDaemon.sendAngle (stepHead :266-287).
findings.estimatedCost: Bounded leak — each settle self-clears when the head reaches center (seconds), so worst case is transient duplicate 10Hz I2C traffic + fighting commands; ~0% steady CPU.
findings.fix: In stopSpeaking, 'if (s.settleTimer) clearInterval(s.settleTimer)' before creating the new one — 1 line.

findings.title: (c) Servo-daemon-down fallback spawns a Python interpreter PER 80ms TRANSITION FRAME
findings.evidence: Eased transitions issue one batchMoveServos per frame at FRAME_INTERVAL_MS=80 (services/movement/transitionEngine.js:96,511-519). When the servo daemon is unreachable, both the single path (hardwareService/index.js:781, spawn at :830-832) and the batch path ('Spawning servo_cli.py per batch is kept as the fallback', index.js:2249-2252) fall back to one-shot servo_cli.py, which the code itself documents as 'seconds each on a Pi 4, re-initialising the chip' (index.js:788-791). With idle poses enabled and the daemon dead, that is a serial python spawn roughly every 1-2s, continuously, all night.
findings.estimatedCost: ~50-100% of one core sustained while the daemon is down and any motion loop (idle poses, head tracking, speech expression) is enabled; also thrashes the PCA9685 (each spawn re-inits the chip). Zero when the daemon is healthy (socket writes <1ms).
findings.fix: Rate-limit or disable eased frame-stepping when servoDaemonClient reports unavailable (it already caches the failure, servoDaemonClient.js:35-44): degrade to ONE direct command per pose instead of 25 frames, and log loudly. On the live node, verify the daemon is actually up (grep .err for 'Servo daemon unavailable').

findings.title: (c) Lurk motion watcher degraded mode spawns python3 gpio_read.py every second
findings.evidence: Degraded fallback: setInterval(pollSensor, pollIntervalMs=1000) (services/lurkMotionWatcherService.js:31,72,260-264) → execFile('/usr/bin/python3', [gpio_read.py, pin]) per tick (:279). Entered after 3 rapid watcher failures (:242-246); the overlap guard (:271) prevents stacking but not the per-second interpreter cost.
findings.estimatedCost: Python interpreter start on a Pi 4B is ~250-500ms CPU → 25-50% of one core sustained while degraded and lurk is on. Healthy mode is a single persistent watcher process (near-zero).
findings.fix: In degraded mode, drop the poll rate to 3-5s (PIR wake latency of a lurking prop tolerates it) or re-attempt the persistent watcher periodically instead of polling forever.

findings.title: (c)+(d) Stall-guard sweep: one servo_cli.py reconcile spawn every 5 minutes
findings.evidence: startPeriodicStallSweep(characterId, 300000) at server.js:238; each tick runs runServoCli(['reconcile', address]) — a fresh python3 spawn (services/hardwareService/stallGuard.js:50-73,161-166), plus one more spawn per channel it releases (:117).
findings.estimatedCost: ~1-2.5s of one core per 5min ≈ 0.3-0.8% average. Justified backstop (fuse-protection), guard prevents duplication (:161).
findings.fix: None needed for CPU; optionally lengthen to 10min. Keep — it exists for a real recurring hardware failure.

findings.title: (d) Idle/random-pose engine cost: per-FRAME re-reads of config, parts.json, model registry and calibration — uncached in the motion hot path
findings.evidence: Every eased frame (12.5Hz during 2s transitions) calls batchMoveServos, which per call does: readConfig (uncached fs read, services/configService.js:12-14, called index.js:2093,2115), parts.json read+JSON.parse (index.js:2122-2131), and PER PART: getModelDefaultsForPart — an uncached model-registry file read+parse (index.js:105-159, called :2162) — plus calStore.get (:2169) and getPartSafety (cached 30s, safetyLimits.js:42-44). Micro-motion adds the same via transitionServos(stepped:false) at 4Hz (idleLoopService.js:171-205 → transitionEngine.js:475-484,538-545). getPhysicalFault IS cached 30s (safetyLimits.js:56-70).
findings.estimatedCost: With a 4-servo pose: ~(1 config + 1 parts + 4 model + 4 cal) reads x 12.5Hz ≈ 125 file-read+parse ops/s during transitions — page-cache hits so mostly JSON.parse CPU, ~5-10% of one core for the 2s of each transition, recurring every 5-10s, all night. Not the box-killer, but the largest steady Node-side consumer when 'random poses' are on.
findings.fix: Cache parts.json and the model registries with the same 30s-TTL pattern safetyLimits already uses (invalidate on write), or resolve the per-part plan ONCE per transition and reuse it for all frames.

findings.title: (d, grows over time) Movement telemetry auto-flush rewrites a growing pretty-printed JSON file every 30s
findings.evidence: startAutoFlush(30000) at server.js:965-967; flush() reads the whole data/movement-telemetry.json, JSON.parses it, merges, and rewrites with JSON.stringify(merged, null, 2) — non-atomic writeFile — every 30s whenever any servo command was recorded (services/movement/movementTelemetry.js:52-100). Cap is 5000 entries (:15) so the file grows to ~0.7-1MB and then every flush is a full ~1MB read+parse+stringify+write. Every servo command records latency entries (servoCommandBuffer.js:178, transitionEngine.js:565-566), so with idle poses/head tracking on, flushes fire every 30s indefinitely.
findings.estimatedCost: ~50-150ms CPU per flush once at cap (≈0.3-0.5% average) + ~2-3GB/day SD write amplification — this is the background item whose cost GROWS over time (until the 5000-entry cap, then plateaus). Also non-atomic: power cut mid-write truncates the file.
findings.fix: Write compact JSON (spaces:0), keep the merged array in RAM between flushes instead of re-reading the file each time, use writeJsonAtomic (already in the repo, services/atomicStore.js), and lengthen the interval to 5min.

findings.title: (d) Head tracking drives up to ~25 controlPart calls/sec through the full per-command lookup stack
findings.evidence: The tracker prints status lines at up to 25/s (output_interval = 1/25, scripts/motion_tracking_service.py:940,976-979); every line triggers maybeDriveHead (controllers/motionTrackingController.js:419) which calls hardwareService.controlPart(...moveToAngle) (motionTrackingController.js:112) — each controlPart repeating the parts/model/calibration resolution described above before the daemon socket write.
findings.estimatedCost: ~5-10% of one core while a target is held (deadzone suppresses commands when still). Additive with the idle-pose engine.
findings.fix: Same caching fix as batchMoveServos; optionally cap head-drive command rate to 10/s (the head is slew-limited anyway).

findings.title: Per-request middleware does 2 file reads + JSON.parse on EVERY request, multiplied by 1Hz dashboard polling
findings.evidence: Global middleware re-reads config/app-config.json (loadConfig) and data/characters.json per request (server.js:403-447). The dashboard polls: activity-status every 1000ms (public/js/dashboard.js:408 → routes/conversation.js:1328, which itself re-reads parts.json), head-tracking-status every 1000ms (dashboard.js:1379 → conversation.js:193-206, another parts.json read), motion-status every 3000ms (dashboard.js:492), console tail every 3000ms when the live-console pane is on — each console poll forks 'tail -n' (dashboard.js:1937 → systemService.js:589-609), character check every 10s (dashboard.js:843).
findings.estimatedCost: One open dashboard ≈ 2.5 req/s ≈ 7-8 file read+parse ops/s (~1-3% core, page-cache-served) + a tail(1) fork every 3s (~2-3% core) when console live is enabled. Two viewers double it. Not fatal, but it is constant load the Pi pays for a page nobody may be watching.
findings.fix: Cache app-config.json/characters.json with a short TTL or fs.watch-free mtime check; have activity-status reuse the parts list it loaded 1s ago.

findings.title: MJPEG proxies have NO frame dropping and duplicate the upstream per client — the design-level latency mechanism for stalled viewers
findings.evidence: Local proxy: streamMJPEG opens a NEW connection to mjpg-streamer per client request and pipes bytes verbatim (controllers/webcamController.js:602-608,676). Fleet proxy: orchestration webcam-stream opens a NEW axios stream to the remote node per viewer and pipes (routes/api/orchestrationRoutes.js:618-676: response.data.pipe(res)), so a fleet view is browser→hub-node→target-node→mjpg-streamer, two Node byte-copy hops. Neither hop parses frames, so neither can drop stale ones: pipe backpressure just pauses the upstream socket and lag accumulates in kernel buffers for that client.
findings.estimatedCost: CPU per viewer per hop ~1-3% core at 640x480@15fps (~0.5-1MB/s memcpy through JS). Latency: unbounded for a slow client — this is a secondary 5s-lag source independent of the tracker; N viewers = N camera-stream duplications on the Pi's wifi.
findings.fix: Smallest honest fix: none in Node for direct viewing (point the straight at :8090 on-LAN); for the proxy, parse the multipart boundary and forward only the newest complete JPEG when the client socket is writable (latest-frame relay), or a single shared upstream tee.

findings.title: Perf console monitor + performance collector: subprocess-based sampling, correctly throttled, ~0.5% core
findings.evidence: 5s interval with heavy work gated to every 12th tick in production (server.js:988-1015): pipewireService.listActiveStreams execs 'wpctl status' (pipewireService.js:667-670) + mjpg health fetch (server.js:999). Performance collector every 300s execs "top -bn1 | grep | awk" (systemService.js:30-35 — top -bn1 alone is ~300-500ms on a Pi), 'df /' (:67-70), thermal sysfs read (:49-55); history flushed to SD once/hour (systemService.js:103-114). Both guarded against duplication (server.js single onServerReady; systemService.js:174).
findings.estimatedCost: ~0.5% of one core combined. The 'top -bn1' choice is the only wart — it is the most expensive way to read CPU% and the code already has the cheap os.cpus() fallback (:36-47).
findings.fix: Use the os.cpus() delta path as primary and drop the top(1) exec.

findings.title: Node discovery browse forks avahi-browse every 30s — modest but forever
findings.evidence: setInterval(browse, 30000) (services/nodeDiscoveryService.js:27,314), each tick exec's 'avahi-browse -rpt _monsterbox._tcp' (:186). Guarded against duplication (:311), unref'd (:315).
findings.estimatedCost: One fork+exec per 30s, ~100-300ms CPU incl. avahi resolution ≈ 0.5-1% of one core average. Acceptable; listed for completeness of (a).
findings.fix: None required; could stretch to 60s (staleAfterMs is 90s, i.e. 3 cycles — adjust together).

findings.title: Dormant-but-real timer sources confirmed NOT running at boot (checked so the synthesizer can exclude them)
findings.evidence: ai/integrations AIPerformanceMonitor/AIClientManager/APIKeyManager intervals (ai/integrations/AIPerformanceMonitor.js:392-410 etc.) are not imported by server.js/routes/services (grep found no references outside ai/integrations). services/goblinService.js beacon (:296) is the goblin-DEVICE side, not imported by the node server. autoAIService timers exist only after an operator enables auto-AI (services/autoAIService.js:45). audioLoopService 5s monitor only while a loop plays (audioLoopService.js:212-216). elevenLabsRealtimeSTTService keepalive (:418) is session-scoped. servoCommandBuffer 50Hz flush loop starts on demand and skips work when queue is empty (servoCommandBuffer.js:222-240).
findings.estimatedCost: 0 at steady state.
findings.fix: None.
